Your favorite route stays beside a cliff, but one random exploratory move can still make you fall. Should the value of that route include those random moves? We will hold one next-state row fixed and calculate three answers. The distinction follows Sutton and Barto, §§5.5 and 6.4–6.6.

Part 4. A value estimate gives credit to earlier actions for rewards that arrive later. But which later actions does it assume? That choice separates on-policy from off-policy learning. We can see the difference without changing the task, the rewards or the table.

Reading goal: keep the next-state row fixed. Changing only the assumed future policy gives targets of 8, a sampled 8 or −10, and an average of 6.2.

Two policies, one task

Suppose you want the shortest route to a goal, and you occasionally try a random move to discover better routes. The rule collecting those moves is the behavior policy, written bbb. The rule whose future you want to value is the target policy, written π\piπ. A vertical bar means “given this state.” Both give action probabilities in a state: b(a∣s)b(a\mid s)b(a∣s) and π(a∣s)\pi(a\mid s)π(a∣s), for action aaa in state sss.

At one illustrative state Right Down
Behavior bbb: collects moves 0.9 0.1
Target π\piπ: greedy continuation 1 0

Here a down move can enter the data even though the future being valued always chooses right. The next section keeps this row and makes the consequences numerical.

If the target and behavior rules match, learning is on-policy. If they differ, it is off-policy. Q-learning can learn after every fresh move and still be off-policy: an exploratory rule acts, while the target assumes greedy continuation. Old data aren't required.

Separating the rules is useful when exploration helps collect information but you want values for a different eventual behavior. It also creates an obligation: the collected data must support the future you're asking about. Sutton and Barto, §5.5.

One row, three targets

Should the backup use the best next move, the move actually drawn, or an average over the policy? Keep the estimates fixed to isolate that choice.

Exploration has a cost

The shortest route can run beside a cliff. With perfectly greedy execution, staying on that route is fine. With continuing exploration, a random downward action can cause a fall, even after the preferred action is well learned.

Q-learning's greedy continuation target values a future without those exploratory deviations. On-policy Sarsa includes them in the behavior it evaluates. So it can prefer a longer route that leaves room to recover. The book's cliff example illustrates this mechanism with persistent exploration. A particular finite run also depends on initialization, visits and learning rate. Example 6.6.

Neither target supplies a physical safety guarantee. Sarsa learns an expected return for its policy, which may still choose dangerous actions. Changing the exploration rule changes that return. Gradually removing exploration changes the comparison again: the book's asymptotic optimality discussion assumes the required exploration and learning-rate conditions.

Data must cover the question

Suppose a stored dataset never takes a bridge that the target policy would use. Replaying the other transitions more often won't reveal where the bridge leads. For action correction, the coverage requirement is that a target action with positive probability also has positive behavior probability.

For a visited state sss and candidate action aaa, that requirement is π(a∣s)>0  ⟹  b(a∣s)>0\pi(a\mid s)>0\;\Longrightarrow\;b(a\mid s)>0π(a∣s)>0⟹b(a∣s)>0. The implication arrow means every action the target might take must be possible under behavior too. Action coverage at a visited state is only part of the problem. The relevant states must also appear in the updates. A buffer can omit them or sample them very unevenly. That distinction matters when a shared formula changes predictions outside the sampled states.

Designed for: off-policy methods let the policy being evaluated differ from the data collector, including a past policy or another controller. Cost: that freedom makes coverage and sampling distribution part of the learning problem. Age alone tells you neither whether data are off-policy nor whether they are useful. §5.5.

Correcting action probabilities

Suppose the data choose right and down equally, but the target chooses right four times as often as down. An unweighted average answers the wrong policy question. Importance weights correct each action's contribution to the average.

At one fixed state sss, let AAA be an action sampled from bbb. Let f(s,a)f(s,a)f(s,a) be any fixed quantity attached to action aaa, and let ρ(a∣s)=π(a∣s)/b(a∣s)\rho(a\mid s)=\pi(a\mid s)/b(a\mid s)ρ(a∣s)=π(a∣s)/b(a∣s) be its importance ratio, where the denominator is positive for target actions. The symbols E\mathbb EE and ∑\sum∑ mean expectation and sum over actions; A∼bA\sim bA∼b means sampling AAA from behavior at this fixed state.

EA∼b[ρ(A∣s)f(s,A)]=∑aπ(a∣s)f(s,a).\mathbb E_{A\sim b}[\rho(A\mid s)f(s,A)]=\sum_a\pi(a\mid s)f(s,a). EA∼b​[ρ(A∣s)f(s,A)]=a∑​π(a∣s)f(s,a).

The reason is cancellation: multiplying behavior probability by the ratio leaves target probability.

For an illustrative calculation, take behavior probabilities (0.5,0.5)(0.5,0.5)(0.5,0.5), target probabilities (0.8,0.2)(0.8,0.2)(0.8,0.2) and quantities (10,−10)(10,-10)(10,−10). The ratios are 1.61.61.6 and 0.40.40.4. Then 0.5(1.6)(10)+0.5(0.4)(−10)=60.5(1.6)(10)+0.5(0.4)(-10)=60.5(1.6)(10)+0.5(0.4)(−10)=6, matching 0.8(10)+0.2(−10)0.8(10)+0.2(-10)0.8(10)+0.2(−10).

Action Behavior Target Ratio Quantity Weighted contribution
Right 0.5 0.8 1.6 10 8
Down 0.5 0.2 0.4 −10 −2

Add the last column to recover 6. Each contribution is behavior probability × ratio × quantity; it is not a new transition or reward.

This is a conditional, one-step action identity. Correcting a whole multi-step return needs the appropriate sequence of ratios, coverage and variance control. Rare behavior actions can receive huge weights. The arithmetic doesn't repair an omitted state or establish convergence for a nonlinear bootstrap learner. §5.5.

Which guarantees survive?

In the drawing, www is a vector of shared model weights. On-policy sampling fixes one distribution mismatch. The familiar convergence result is more specific: fixed-policy prediction with fixed linear features, suitable visits and diminishing learning rates. A changing control policy and a nonlinear network need their own analysis. Tsitsiklis and Van Roy, 1997.

Method Continuation in the target Primary source
Q-learning Largest next-action estimate §6.5
Sarsa One action sampled from its policy §6.4
Expected Sarsa Average under the chosen target policy §6.6

A short Expected Sarsa loop makes the policy choice explicit. As above, St,At,Rt+1S_t,A_t,R_{t+1}St​,At​,Rt+1​ are the current state, sampled action and following reward; YtY_tYt​ is the target, α\alphaα the update fraction, bbb collects actions and π\piπ weights their continuation. In the code, gamma, alpha and pi spell those same symbols:

choose A_t using behavior b at S_t
observe R_(t+1), S_(t+1), terminal
if terminal: Y_t = R_(t+1)
else: Y_t = R_(t+1) + gamma * sum_a pi(a|S_(t+1)) Q(S_(t+1),a)
move Q(S_t,A_t) a fraction alpha toward Y_t

Here terminal means the episode ended, so there is no remaining value to bootstrap.

  • On-policy benefit: the target includes the behavior's exploratory costs.
  • Off-policy benefit: collection and the policy being learned about can differ.
  • Coverage cost: missing actions or states leave parts of the question unsupported.
  • Approximation limit: shared predictions can feed changes back into their own targets.

From action credit to a policy update

How do we turn those values into a better action rule? Generalized Advantage Estimation (GAE) estimates whether an action did better or worse than the policy's state-value baseline, using a mixture of return lengths. Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) can use that credit to train the policy. Its clipped objective limits the incentive to change an action's probability too far relative to the policy that collected the rollout. Clipping does not impose a hard bound on the policy step. GAE supplies action credit; PPO clipping shapes the update incentive. Spinning Up's PPO explanation.
